tool.name: CodeTrace
tool.description: compiler-driven program dependency and vulnerability analysis

language.dialect: C-like subset parsed by a canonical LR(1) / LALR(1) parser

dispositions.note: A sink call appears here when no enabled flow connects a configured source to it, when the required taint context was removed by a declared sanitizer, or when the statement sits in a branch whose literal condition makes it unreachable.

source.description: one line read from standard input; attacker controlled in most deployments

findings.feasibility_note: no branch condition guards the reported path; the path is structurally reachable from the entry of the enclosing function.
findings.explanation: Potential command injection flow detected: data introduced at line 8 (input) reaches argument 0 of system() at line 10, which rule 'command_system' classifies as a 'command' context operation. The taint engine propagated the atom(s) src:stdin@command along 7 recorded step(s): input() introduces untrusted data (source rule 'stdin') (line 8) -> 'name' is assigned a tainted value at line 8 (line 8) -> argument 0 of the call to build_command() is tainted (line 9) -> 'user_input' is a parameter of build_command() (line 3) -> build_command() returns a tainted value (line 4) -> call to build_command() propagates taint to the caller (line 9) -> 'command' is assigned a tainted value at line 9 (line 9). The flow crosses at least one function boundary, so the interprocedural summary was used. The flow rule 'command_execution' connects source 'stdin' to sink 'command_system' and lists sanitizers shell_escape, parse_to_int, validate_command; none of them removed the atoms that reached this sink. Analysis certainty: approximate. This is a static finding: exploitability was not established.
limitations: Interprocedural reasoning is context-insensitive: parameters are summarised across all call sites, which can add flows that a single call site cannot actually create.
The flow was detected by static analysis only; the analysed program was never executed and exploitability was not established.
findings.remediation: Do not build a command from untrusted input. Prefer a fixed program path with arguments passed as separate values; if a shell string is unavoidable, escape the value for the command context (for example with the 'shell_escape' rule) and re-run the analysis to confirm the flow disappears.

evidence.taint_engine: context-insensitive, flow-sensitive may-analysis over the CFG
evidence.reaching_definitions: used to justify each data-flow hop in the path

notes: Interprocedural propagation is context-insensitive: a parameter that is tainted at one call site is analysed as tainted at every call site of that function.
limitations: Static analysis only: the analysed program is never executed. A reported flow means the analysis could not exclude it, not that it is exploitable.
The supported language subset is documented in docs/LANGUAGE.md; constructs outside it are reported as unsupported and are not analysed.
Interprocedural reasoning is context-insensitive: a parameter tainted at one call site is summarised as tainted for every call site.
Pointers, aliasing, dynamic memory, structs, and the preprocessor are outside the supported subset and are never assumed safe.
Array elements are not tracked individually; taint assigned to one element is attributed to the whole array.
Sanitizers are only trusted where a rule declares them, and only for the declared context; unknown functions are never assumed to validate their arguments.

A branch guarded by a rule-declared validator suppresses the flows through that branch: the validator's implementation is not analysed, so the run assumes it rejects every value that is unsafe for its context. Every such suppression is listed in guard_suppressions.
Reports contain the results of the run they were produced from; re-running after editing the source or the rules produces a new, independent report.
